CHECK 3 <- REFUTER "a trivial f works" (e.g. a bump function, or a polynomial, with all unit-sphere integrals zero)

Any nonzero f must have some unit sphere with nonzero integral unless it is a genuinely special function. A bump supported in a ball of radius < 1 integrates to zero on spheres that miss it, but spheres of radius 1 centred near it still cross it with nonzero integral generically. A polynomial with all unit-sphere integrals zero would have to be a nontrivial solution of the spherical-mean equation, which is the hard part of the problem. Checking this by computation would require the same analysis.

RESULT 3: no trivial witness identified. A counterexample needs a nontrivial construction for radius-1 spheres in R^3, and Mathlib provides none of the required machinery (surface integrals over spheres are present, but no spherical-mean inversion or construction).
